---
title: BioCloud
order: 4
---

BioCloud is a CPU cluster at AAU, with nodes that have many cores and a large
amount of memory each, along with a single node with two GPUs. It is the
natural place for CPU calculations, e.g. DFT, sampling with machine-learned
potentials and data processing, while GPU work such as training models is
better placed on [AI Cloud](aicloud.qmd).

This page assumes that you have read the pages on [SSH](ssh.qmd) and
[Slurm](slurm.qmd), and it only describes what is specific to BioCloud. The
[BioCloud documentation](https://docs.biocloud.bio.aau.dk/) asks that new
users read all of it, which is well worth doing; it is not long.

## Access

Access is granted to your AAU account by a BioCloud administrator, as
described in the
[introduction](https://docs.biocloud.bio.aau.dk/) of the documentation. Once
it has been granted, you can log in with `ssh biocloud` using the
configuration from the [SSH page](ssh.qmd).

In addition to SSH, BioCloud has a
[web portal](https://docs.biocloud.bio.aau.dk/access/webportal/) at
<https://biocloud.bio.aau.dk>, from where Jupyter, VS Code, RStudio and a
virtual desktop can be started as jobs on a compute node. Like SSH, it
requires the AAU network or the VPN.

## Storage

| Location | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
| `/home/<user>` | Your own files and individual projects. |
| `/projects` | Projects shared between several people, organised as `/projects/<PI>/<project>`. |
| `/tmp` on a compute node | Fast local scratch space for a running job, deleted when your last job on the node ends. |

Both `/home` and `/projects` are on the same network storage, which is shared
by all nodes, such that files written on the login node are available in jobs
and vice versa. Two properties of this storage are worth knowing from the
start:

- **Nothing is backed up.** A deleted file cannot be recovered. Code belongs
  in git, and results that matter should be copied elsewhere.
- **Many small files are slow.** The storage handles a few large files well,
  but directories with tens of thousands of small files, such as Python
  environments, put a load on it. This is the reason BioCloud recommends
  containers, see [Software](#software) below.

Local scratch space is only available on some nodes, and is requested with
`--constraint scratch`; the
[local scratch page](https://docs.biocloud.bio.aau.dk/storage/local/)
describes how to use it.

## Partitions

BioCloud chooses the partition for a batch job itself, and `--partition` has
no effect on batch jobs. It prefers the partitions in the order of the table
below, using the next one when the first has no room.
Knowing the partitions is therefore mostly useful for
understanding where a job ended up and how large a single job can be.

| Partition | Nodes | Cores | Memory | Max time | Billing | Purpose |
|-----------|------:|------:|-------:|---------:|--------:|---------|
| `zen5` | 5 | 1376 | 7550 GB | 14 days | 1.0 | Batch jobs, first choice |
| `zen3` | 6 | 1216 | 6036 GB | 14 days | 0.5 | Batch jobs |
| `zen5x` | 2 | 576 | 4532 GB | 14 days | 1.5 | Batch jobs, more memory per node |
| `zen3x` | 2 | 448 | 4004 GB | 14 days | 1.0 | Batch jobs, more memory per node |
| `interactive` | 1 | 192 | 502 GB | 1 day | 0.5 | Interactive jobs and the web portal |
| `gpu-a10` | 1 | 64 | 250 GB | 14 days | 0.5 + 16 per GPU | Jobs that use a GPU (2 × NVIDIA A10) |

The cores and memory are totals for the partition; a single job is limited by
what is available on one node, unless it uses MPI across several nodes. The
cores are counted as Slurm counts them, i.e. as hardware threads, which is
twice the number of physical cores. The default time limit is one hour in all
partitions.

The billing factor determines how much a job counts towards your account's
usage, which in turn lowers the priority of your next jobs: an hour on 10
cores counts as 10 core hours on `zen5`, 5 on `zen3` and 15 on `zen5x`. Each
GPU hour adds another 16, such that the GPU node should only be used by jobs that
actually use the GPU. The
[accounting page](https://docs.biocloud.bio.aau.dk/slurm/accounting/) describes
how priority is calculated.

The table reflects the cluster in November 2026. The current state is shown
with

```bash
sinfo -s
scontrol show partition
```

## Software

BioCloud recommends containers, run with
[Apptainer](https://docs.biocloud.bio.aau.dk/software/containers/), for most
software, because an environment inside a container is a single file on the
network storage rather than tens of thousands. Conda (with `mamba`) is
installed and configured as well, and is described on the
[conda page](https://docs.biocloud.bio.aau.dk/software/conda/).

In practice, an environment in the project directory, e.g. with
[Pixi](../tools/pixi.qmd) or uv, is fine for development and a moderate number
of jobs. When a project grows to many jobs or many users, building a
container from the same environment is the more considerate choice; the
[Containers](containers.qmd) page describes how.

Two rules from the BioCloud documentation are easy to miss:

- Containers are built on the login node, not inside a Slurm job.
- Container images are always referenced with a specific version tag, never
  `latest`, such that the same job gives the same result later.

## A job on BioCloud

A minimal job script for a project that uses Pixi looks as follows:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/bash -l
#SBATCH --job-name=fit
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%j.out
#SBATCH --time=0-02:00:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=16G

export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
pixi run python fit.py
```

The `-l` on the first line makes the job load the same shell setup as a
login, which BioCloud requires for conda to work in jobs and which does no
harm otherwise. No `--partition` is needed, as explained above. After the job
has finished, `seff <jobid>` shows whether the requested cores and memory
were used.

## Rules that are easy to break

- No calculations on the login nodes, however small; this includes running a
  Jupyter kernel or a test script there.
- In VS Code, open a project folder rather than your whole home directory,
  otherwise VS Code indexes the home directory on the login node.
- Do not leave interactive jobs or web portal sessions running when they are
  not in use.
- Do not use the GPU node for jobs that only use CPUs.
- Delete data that is no longer needed; the storage is not meant for long-term
  storage.
